transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
The U.S. and Israel are drawing up plans for possibly another attack on Iran after the
midterms, according to a person briefed on the war planning, and PR's Ruth Sherlock
has details.
Well, a source who spoke on condition of anonymity so they could discuss the preparations with
NPR says Israel had initially planned to strike Iran in mid-October about two weeks before
Israeli elections, but President Trump objected.
The source said the U.S., though, is now amassing forces in the region to be ready for an attack
by early November after the U.S. midterms.
But you know, nothing here is for certain.
They also said these preparations could be part of a campaign to pressure Iran to reach
a diplomatic deal.
NPR's Ruth Sherlock.
The battle for votes has kicked into high gear with less than two weeks to go before
the midterms.
President Trump is the most prominent Republican to crisscross the country in a bid to keep
Congress and the GOP's control, and the Democratic Party's most prominent figures are also campaigning
to keep that from happening.
And Pierre Stephen Fowler takes us to Mississippi.
Former Vice President Kamala Harris is campaigning for Democratic Senate nominee Scott Colom in
what has become yet another race in a deep-bred state that could be competitive.
His top voices in the party also fan out to Arkansas, Alabama and other key races.
Several Democrats with possible 2028 presidential interests have done campaign swings throughout
the South in recent days, as early voting data shows a notable bump in black voter turnout.
Former President Obama hits the stump in Ohio and Michigan this weekend, and Georgia next
week where all three have competitive governor and Senate races.
Stephen Fowler, NPR News, South Haven, Mississippi.
Weapons are divided over an attack ad by Vivek Ramaswamy.
He is running for governor in Ohio and recently put out an ad featuring the estranged mother
of his Democratic rival, Amy Acton, calling her daughter a liar.
Acton's stepfather was charged with raping her as a child and she was removed from her
mother's care.
That was not mentioned in the ad.
A sell-off in AI stocks such as meta pummeled stock markets, sending the tech-heavy Nasdaq
down more than 2%, and Pierre's Rafael Naum has a look at an ugly day on Wall Street.
It's becoming a well-known sequence.
AI stocks rally for a while amid hopes about game-changing technology, only to then suffer
big sell-offs as investors get skittish about how much money is being spent across the sector.
The latest example is meta.
Its shares plunged after the company said they would need to continue increasing spending
on AI, including unbuilding data centers.
Other AI stocks are also down sharply, including Nvidia.
Rafael Naum, NPR News.
Let's check out the stocks.
The Nasdaq is down 694 points, or 2.6% at the close.
The S&P has fallen 93 and the Dow ends the day up 11 points.
You're listening to NPR News.
Mortgage rates declined for the first time in more than two months, according to Freddie
Mac.
But, and Pierre-Steven Bassaha reports, rates are still much higher than they were a year
ago and keeping would-be homebuyers on the sidelines.
Mortgage rates fell this week to 7.32%, a small dip from last week.
This is for an average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage.
Kate Wood is Nerdwall's housing expert and says this does not necessarily mean rates
have turned a corner.
"Seeing, okay, this is the first decrease that we've had after weeks of increases.
Like, yes, it's exciting, but I say all the time mortgage rates do not follow the laws
of gravity.
What goes up does not have to come down."
The fundamentals that have pushed mortgage rates up have not changed much.
Inflation is still high, and mortgage rates are still more than a full percentage point
higher than they were a year ago.
Steven Bassaha, NPR News.
A historic World War II era globe linked to President Dwight D. Eisenhower now has a gash.
NPR's Quill Lawrence reports Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's staff accidentally damaged
it.
General and later President Eisenhower is seen next to maps or oversized globes in many
historic photos associated with the D-Day invasion during World War II.
Hegseth had requested one of those globes be moved into his office and it got damaged
in the process last February, according to a U.S. official not authorized to speak publicly,
who tells NPR that "Antarctica has a hole in it."
The story was first reported by the Washington Post, which published a photo of the damaged
globe.
The Pentagon press office sent a statement confirming that an accident had occurred and
said the globe was a replica and that it was being repaired.
Quill Lawrence, NPR News.

topics.text: U.S. and Israel draw up plans for possible second attack on Iran after midterms
Trump and Democratic figures ramp up campaigning with less than two weeks before midterms
Vivek Ramaswamy's Ohio governor ad attacking Amy Acton's mother draws criticism
AI stock sell-off sends Nasdaq down 2.6% after Meta spending warnings
Mortgage rates dip for first time in two months but remain well above last year
Damaged Eisenhower-linked World War II globe at Hegseth's Pentagon office, Antarctica gashed
